summary.text: A 72-year-old woman with a history of gastritis and urinary incontinence presented with depressed level of consciousness after one day of confusion and lethargy. She had a fever of 38.6°C without meningismus, psychomotor slowing, impaired attention and clearly visible choreiform movements of the neck and left upper extremity that she could not suppress. Initial tests showed mildly elevated C-reactive protein and an abnormal urinalysis.

She was empirically treated with ceftriaxone, but fevers, impaired attention and chorea persisted despite urine cultures growing E. coli. Lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, oligoclonal bands, increased IgG index and synthesis, and a positive CSF PCR for herpes simplex virus 2. The remaining infectious workup, the Mayo CSF autoimmune panel and MR brain were negative or unremarkable, and the serum autoimmune panel was omitted.

Acyclovir was started without notable improvement. On hospital day six a parainfectious CNS autoimmunity was suspected and IVIG was started, then discontinued after two sessions because of severe hypotension. Plasmapheresis began on hospital day 9, with significant improvement of chorea after one session and complete resolution after the fourth; she received five sessions and three weeks of acyclovir.

Mental status improved only minimally by discharge to acute rehabilitation on hospital day 27. She completed rehabilitation and returned to the neurology clinic three months after discharge, with complete recovery and no neurological sequelae.

ambiguities.issue: An initial urinalysis was positive for leukocyte esterase, bacteria and white blood cells, while a later sentence among the work-up reported after the lumbar puncture states that urinalysis did not reveal any signs of infection. The source does not say whether the second is a repeat test or when it was done, and does not identify the two as the same test, so they are kept as separate observations without ordering and not treated as a source conflict.

evidence.quote: The patient was found to have a urinalysis that was positive for leukocyte esterase, bacteria, and white blood cells.
Urinalysis did not reveal any signs of infection.

ambiguities.issue: Whether concurrent CNS autoimmunity contributed to the chorea is unresolved: it was suspected on hospital day six, and the authors conclude only a possible autoimmune cause of chorea can be diagnosed, since serum neuronal autoantibody testing was omitted. No confirmed autoimmune diagnosis is inferred.

evidence.quote: we may only, at best, fulfill a diagnosis of a possible autoimmune cause of chorea
Serum autoimmune encephalitis panel was inadvertently omitted.
